fieldData.excerpt: Bulgaria was the 88th country. Anton, the retired physics teacher, ordered plum brandy at nine in the morning. The Eurovision voting bloc, he explained, was a Cold War artifact. The soup needed more vinegar. Both opinions were correct.
fieldData.body:
🇧🇬 Anton orders the plum brandy for both of us at nine in the morning and tells me, before I have removed my coat, that the Eurovision voting bloc is a Cold War artifact and that the soup needs more vinegar.

Both opinions are correct.

Anton is a retired physics teacher in Sofia who now runs a Saturday-morning conversation circle at Cafe Pesho's, two streets behind the Saint Sofia statue. He is 73, wears the kind of cardigan you cannot buy in airports, and has a Bulgarian shepherd named Pepi who watches the room from a folded blanket near the radiator. Pepi has opinions too. Pepi keeps them to himself.

Why Bulgaria was on the spreadsheet

I am here because Bulgaria was the eighty-eighth country, and because Jay has gone to find the parking, and because a woman at the next table is laughing at her phone in a way that suggests the joke is not safe for work.

The Trip Ledger, my husband Jay calls it. A Google Sheet I have maintained since 2008, when we were broke and lived in a sublet in Brooklyn and could only count the Mexican border crossings as international travel. Now the sheet has eight tabs, a Visited filter, an opinion column, and a hidden conditional format that turns a country green when I have eaten breakfast there. (Lunch and dinner do not count. They are too easy.)

Bulgaria is the 88th row. The Balkans country that finally undid the structure. Not because of breakfast. Because of Anton.

How to get to Anton's cafe from the airport

The cab from Sofia Airport runs about 30 leva, the equivalent of fifteen American dollars or a bad oat milk latte in Copenhagen. The driver is a former IT consultant named Petar who quit during the pandemic to drive his own car and read more. Petar recommends three things, unprompted: the Banya Bashi mosque, the Saint Sofia statue, and a tarator place near the National Theatre that uses sparkling water in the broth. Anton, he notes, would approve.

Petar drops me at Pesho's and refuses a tip in the way Bulgarian drivers do, which is by accepting it eventually after a small, choreographed protest. He is reading a book by Georgi Gospodinov in the front seat. He tells me his daughter is at university in Plovdiv studying agricultural science. She has not been to Eurovision but has firm opinions on the Greek voting bloc inherited from her grandmother.

Sofia is a city that has been repainted, then unrepainted, then mostly repainted, in the time since 1989. The Banya Bashi mosque sits across from a Sofia statue that used to be a Lenin statue. The National Theatre is the building you see on every postcard of Sofia and which appears on the magnets at the airport. Nobody who lives in Sofia photographs it. Petar told me this with the gentle weariness of a man who has driven enough tourists.

(Anton, when I mention the photographing, says: of course. We do not photograph our own dining table.)

The plum brandy at 9am

The plum brandy is called rakia. It arrives in glasses too small for ceremony and too full for politeness. Anton lifts his. We say наздраве. He is satisfied. He returns to the topic of the soup.

The soup, when it arrives, is tarator. Cucumber, yogurt, walnut, dill, garlic, the ice cubes that make every American visitor look up from their phone. Anton was right about the vinegar. He fixes it with a small bottle he keeps in his bag. He travels with vinegar. This is the kind of detail that explains a country. Pepi, by the radiator, takes a slow breath. He has seen this before.

Outside, a tram passes, and the radio in the cafe shifts from a 1960s Bulgarian folk song to Erasure's A Little Respect, and Pepi opens one eye. The Eurovision conversation, Anton notes, was always going somewhere.

Jay finds the bakery

By the time we have moved on from the rakia, Jay reappears. He has paid for parking and found a bakery. He has the look of a man who has been allowed to remain in a country.

The bakery is two doors down. The pastry is called mekitsa, which is fried dough with white cheese and powdered sugar, and which Jay has now placed on top of the conversation circle like an offering. Anton, who has eaten thousands of mekitsa in his life, eats this one with respect.

The Bulgarian coffee that follows is, I am not exaggerating, the same density as motor oil and twice as personal. It is served in a thimble. You drink half. You wait. You drink the other half. You leave.

Magnus in Copenhagen, supervising the daylight

Magnus 🐻‍❄️ stays in Copenhagen this trip. The math on a 6.5 hour each-way drive plus a Samoyed who considers any temperature above 22 Celsius a personal insult does not work out. He gets a sitter, three walks a day, and a video call from the airport. He looks unimpressed. The video shows me holding a plastic cup of rakia in front of a window that, in Magnus's view, contains no goats and is therefore not worth turning his head for.

The train out of Sofia

I add Bulgaria to the spreadsheet on the train back to Sofia Airport. 88 countries. 7 continents. 464 cities. 36.97 percent of the world. The spreadsheet ticks over. It does not celebrate. It logs.

The window passes a sunflower field, then a billboard for a pop singer named Azis, then a building that has been repainted, then unrepainted, then mostly repainted, in the time since 1989. Pepi, somewhere in the cafe behind us, is still asleep.

This is what Bulgaria felt like. A breakfast that was also a thesis on what is wrong with the Greek televote. A soup that explained a country. A retired physics teacher who carries vinegar. A dog who watched. A driver who reads.

Where to find Anton (and the soup)

Cafe Pesho's is real but the address is the kind of address that makes Bulgarians laugh. Two streets behind the Saint Sofia statue. Look for the cardigan in the window. If Pepi is not there, the cafe is closed. Anton's Saturday circle starts at 9am sharp, which means 9:23am, which means whenever the rakia is poured.

If you are passing through Sofia, eat at a tarator place that uses sparkling water (Petar's recommendation, near the National Theatre, looks for the green awning). Order the rakia even if it is 9am. Especially if it is 9am.

The Trip Ledger is updated by the time the bread cools.

Bulgaria, the eighty-eighth row.

I am not done.

fieldData.short-version: A long Sofia layover is worth leaving the airport for. The city center is about 30 minutes away, by metro or a roughly 30 leva (around 15 USD) cab. Order rakia (the plum brandy, yes, at nine in the morning), tarator (the cold cucumber, yogurt and walnut soup, and add vinegar), and a mekitsa from the bakery two doors down. Bulgaria was country 88 on the Trip Ledger, and it is the one that finally felt like a celebration.
fieldData.quick-answers:
Is a long Sofia layover worth leaving the airport?

Yes. The center is about 30 minutes away by metro or a short cab ride, so even a half-day connection leaves time for breakfast and a slow walk.

How do I get from Sofia Airport to the center?

Metro Line 1 runs from the airport to the center in roughly 30 minutes, or a cab is about 30 leva (around 15 USD).

What should I order?

Rakia (plum brandy), tarator (cold cucumber and yogurt soup, add vinegar), a mekitsa from a bakery, and a Bulgarian coffee served in a thimble. Drink half, wait, then drink the rest.

Do I need a visa for a short layover?

Most EU and US passport holders do not for a short visit. Always confirm against your own passport before you go.

hero-image.alt: Sofia, Bulgaria, dusk on Vitosha Boulevard, country 88

fieldData.excerpt: 🇧🇬 Sofia, May 9, 2026. Bulgaria, country #88. The long restaurant on Vitosha Boulevard. An eight-year-old in braids named Boryana, a 45-kilo Samoyed named Magnus 🐻‍❄️ Waffles, a plum brandy that arrived without being ordered, and the small mathematics of why a place becomes a place.
fieldData.body:
🇧🇬 Sofia, May 9, 2026. Bulgaria, country #88. We are at a long restaurant on Vitosha Boulevard, which is a pedestrian artery the locals defend the way Parisians defend the Marais, with a low-level affection that turns into a fierce protectiveness if you mispronounce the word for it (Витоша, with the accent on the first syllable, do not say Vee-TO-sha).

The restaurant is named Hadjidraganov's Cellars. The waiter is Aleksandar. The dog is Magnus 🐻‍❄️ Waffles, supervising from a sit-stay under the table. The other dog at the table is not at our table but at the neighboring one: a Bulgarian Shepherd named Vasil, slate-grey, ninety kilos, sleeping the way only a 90-kilo shepherd can sleep, which is to say with full faith that the world will not require him.

The plum brandy that arrived without being ordered

The plum brandy is called rakia. Specifically, slivova rakia, from plums, from the village of Troyan, distilled by a man named Petar whose name is on the bottle in Cyrillic and whose family has been distilling at the same address since 1932. We did not order it. Aleksandar brought it. He brought two glasses, which became three when he sat down for the toast.

The toast was Наздраве (nazdrave), to your health, said three times, with eye contact each time. The Carletons have learned to make eye contact in seventeen different ways, but the Bulgarian way is unbroken and not negotiable. You do not look at the glass. You do not look at the table. You look at the person. If you do not look at the person, the toast does not count, and Aleksandar will not say so, but he will know.

The 88th country, briefly

This is country #88. There is a spreadsheet. The spreadsheet does not lie to itself about what counts as a visit. (A six-hour airport layover does not count. A meal and a walk does. A dinner with a stranger and a toast counts twice.)

The spreadsheet does not know about Boryana yet.

Boryana

Boryana is eight. Boryana has braids. Boryana has a snowman keychain with a wonky carrot nose, which she will eventually hand to Magnus 🐻‍❄️ as a goodbye gift, and which is now on his leash. Boryana has been studying our table since we sat down. The study has been clinical. The decision, when she made it, was final: she came over, gave a small bow to the humans, and went under the table to see the dog.

She sat with Magnus 🐻‍❄️ for forty minutes. She spoke to him in Bulgarian. He listened. (He is good at listening. It is his second-best skill, after sitting.) Her grandmother, whose name is Tsvetanka but who Boryana calls Baba, waved her permission across the room and then waved at me, mother to mother, the kind of wave that means he is fine, she is fine, you can keep eating.

The dinner, briefly

What we ate: a shopska salad (tomato, cucumber, raw onion, the white brined sirene cheese grated like snow on top, the sirene a thing the Bulgarians will fight you about, with reason). A kavarma (slow-cooked pork with onions and paprika in a clay pot, the pot the right shape, the pork the right tenderness, the paprika smoked and not sweet). A banitsa to share (filo, white cheese, eggs, butter, served warm). Three glasses of rakia. One more for Aleksandar, on Aleksandar.

Jay had the wine. Specifically, a Mavrud from Plovdiv, which is a grape only Bulgaria grows seriously, dark and a little wild, the sort of wine that pairs with the kind of dinner that lasts three hours.

How a country becomes a country

Country #88 was technically Bulgaria the moment we walked off the Lufthansa flight from Munich at SOF at 14:32 local. That is the bureaucratic answer. The spreadsheet answer is later: when we sat down at the long table on Vitosha, when Aleksandar refilled the rakia, when Boryana decided, when Tsvetanka waved. A country becomes a country when a person inside it sees you, names you, and gives you something you did not ask for.

Bulgaria gave us the toast, the plum brandy, the eight-year-old, the snowman keychain, and a 90-kilo shepherd sleeping like the world owes him nothing.

The Tokyo Major is in 9 months and 22 days. The training is the project. The 88th country is now a place. Magnus 🐻‍❄️ has the keychain. The keychain is on the leash. The leash is going to country #89 next.

Hadjidraganov's Cellars on Vitosha Boulevard, the pedestrian artery. Order shopska salad, kavarma, and a banitsa to share.

A Bulgarian fruit brandy. This one is slivova rakia, made from plums from the village of Troyan. Toast with nazdrave, three times, eye contact each time.

Tomato, cucumber, and raw onion, topped with white brined sirene cheese grated like snow.

fieldData.excerpt: Christmas in the Brazilian Switzerland: a koi pond, a mud spa, a jungle hillside, and three very muddy beings. Plus how doctors built a Swiss town in Brazil.
fieldData.body:
By Christmas night, all three of us were muddy, and only one of us had done it on purpose.

Snowflakes, traded

We spent Christmas in Campos do Jordão, up in the Serra da Mantiqueira, the town Brazilians call the Suíça Brasileira, the Brazilian Switzerland. Half-timbered hotels, steep roofs, flowerbeds laid out like someone was being graded on them. The town is littered with fondue shops and pancake spots, committed to the Alpine bit even in December. And then, between the chalets, palm trees and tree ferns, and a sky that clearly had not been told it was Christmas. Rolling green valleys, forested ridges, araucárias on every skyline: some of the prettiest countryside I have ever seen.

So: Swiss-German "mountains," Brazilian summer. We traded snowflakes for sunshine and did not miss them once.

The mud report

Magnus Waffles (our Samoyed, then a puppy on his very first Christmas, and roughly the size and color of a cloud) found a koi pond and went in, looking for some big ol' fish. Planned, maybe? He has never confirmed or denied. He came out a different color than he went in.

Jay indulged in a mud spa. In our itinerary it is listed as "Jay's Special Treat (Arrive 15 minutes early)," at the Botanique Hotel & Spa, a lodge of glass and giant river stones up on a hillside outside town. The place is stunning: stone walls, glass to the ceiling, and a terrace of sheepskin-draped chairs looking straight down the valley. It is the only version of getting muddy on this trip that came with a towel and a receipt.

I conquered jungle hillsides like a boss. The hills did not go quietly.

So we were all muddy. Different methods, same result.

Iced coffee, deconstructed

At the spa, I ordered an iced coffee. Brazil is a hot country, so you would think this is a normal request. It is not a common order there, and the staff at Botanique handled it with great creativity: out came a giant, steaming pot of pour-over and, beside it, a cup of ice. Assembly required. It worked, and it meant a lot more coffee for me, which I count as a win.

It went better than it did for my friend, American Jen. Early in her time in Brazil, she walked into a Starbucks in Rio and ordered "café com gelo," which translates literally to coffee with ice. She was handed a cup of coffee and some hand sanitizer.

(Our best guess at the mix-up: gelo is ice, and gel, as in álcool em gel, is hand sanitizer. One syllable stands between you and a cold drink.)

Magnus had a big spa day too, just not the kind with towels. He took his first golf cart ride, sitting up on the back bench like a tiny white dignitary surveying his valley, and then got his first taste of independence, hiking the countryside while Jay lay back and got muddy on purpose.

A matter of perspective

At the Bosque do Silêncio, a private patch of native forest less than two kilometers from the tourist center, there is a heart-shaped frame woven with ferns and red roses, built for exactly the photo you think it was built for. We each took a turn in it with Magnus.

Jay posted the pair with a note that this captured the importance of perspective. His point: I look at Magnus and see our Lille Puppers Bubba Zu, and I am genuinely surprised, every time, when strangers are intimidated by him. Then they meet him, and realize he is a total sweetie and an enormous goofball.

In my photo, I am holding him like a baby. In Jay's, he is up on his hind legs with his paws on the frame, all legs and fluff and tongue. Both photos are accurate. That is the whole problem.

Jay signed off his post: "Merry First Christmas Mags. You're growing super fast and the only thing bigger than you is your derp!" Factually correct.

Christmas, rearranged

We were up the mountain from 22 to 26 December 2023, and the rest of the holiday was gentle.

After Jay's spa morning on the 23rd, the afternoon went to beer: Gård, a small craft brewery, then Baden Baden, the town's classic beer hall. Fittingly, for two people now writing this from Copenhagen, Gård is the Danish word for farm. The brewery was started by two great-grandsons of a Danish engineer, Holger Jensen Kok, whose family land sits right on the edge of what became the state forest park.

Christmas Eve started at Le Chalet. Christmas lunch was at the Ort Hotel, in the neighborhood of Vila Natal. Natal is Portuguese for Christmas, and the brigadier the whole town is named after once renamed his farm here Fazenda Natal. So we had Christmas lunch in, more or less, Christmas Village, on what was once Christmas Farm. You cannot plan that. We did not.

His first Christmas, professionally documented

That December also brought Magnus his first Christmas photo shoot, back in São Paulo with Juliana Cadima of Studio Foto Pet, a pet photography studio in the city's Zona Norte. She was amazing. She got a five-month-old Samoyed to sit still in a Santa hat, hold a plaid bone that reads "Meu 1º Natal" (my first Christmas), pose with the two of us in matching buffalo plaid, and somehow look delighted about all of it. If you are ever in São Paulo with a fluffy family member, find her: @studiofotopet on Instagram.

Twelve gifts, one pair of working feet

One of our Christmas traditions is the 12 days of Christmas: we each get the other 12 gifts. It is, honestly, a symptom of expat life. When your family is an ocean away, the tree looks a little empty otherwise.

That year, Jay was nursing a foot injury and could not carry boxes. So I made about a dozen trips up the mountain stairs, hauling boxes. Some people do stair intervals for fitness. I did them for love, and for the tree.

We also got a huge Brazilian meal box from Casa Santa Luzia, the São Paulo grocer I am frankly obsessed with. It opened in 1926 as a little dry-goods shop in the Jardins and is now a temple of imported everything; its coffee selection alone is off the hook. It was our first time sharing a panettone.

The box itself was gloriously eclectic: grape juice, cans, the works. That turns out to be the point. The cesta de Natal, the Christmas basket, is a Brazilian institution, and companies traditionally hand them out to staff at the end of the year. The classic lineup is a panettone, a bottle of sparkling wine, cider or whole grape juice (the version everyone at the table can drink), a can of peaches in syrup, nuts, dried fruit and chocolates. Ours was the deluxe edition of a box a lot of Brazil gets every December.

The rest was pea soup and warm lattes. Fire pits in the evening, with the air cooling off the way it only does up high. Hammocks in the sun. A daybed under a tree hung with woven lanterns. And video calls home, because when you live abroad, Christmas morning arrives in a few different time zones and you take it in shifts.

It was not the Christmas any of us grew up with. It was a uniquely wonderful one anyway: Christmas in nature, with my two favorite muddy beings.

How a tuberculosis cure built a Swiss town in Brazil

Here is the thing about the Brazilian Switzerland: nobody Swiss built it. Doctors did.

In the late 1800s, the leading treatment for tuberculosis was climatotherapy, the belief that thin, dry mountain air could heal damaged lungs. Campos do Jordão sits at about 1,628 meters, commonly cited as the highest city in Brazil, and physicians began comparing its air to Switzerland's. In 1874, Mateus da Costa Pinto, now counted as the town's founder, bought land along the Imbiri river and opened a boarding house for tuberculosis patients. That boarding house is, more or less, where the town starts.

Getting sick people up the mountain was the problem. Patients made the climb from Pindamonhangaba on horseback, in litters, or in mule-drawn carts. So two public-health doctors from Pindamonhangaba, Emílio Ribas and Victor Godinho, pushed for a railway. The Estrada de Ferro Campos do Jordão opened on 15 November 1914: 47 kilometers, a climb of about 1,000 meters, and no cog rail, just wheels gripping steel up grades steeper than 11 percent. It still runs.

The town grew around the sick. A whole neighborhood, Vila Abernéssia, was built for the sanatoriums. In 1926 the state made Campos do Jordão a "sanitary prefecture," a health resort run on the model of European spa towns, and the center of what planners hoped would be a healing belt across the Mantiqueira.

Then medicine moved on. Once drugs could treat tuberculosis, nobody needed to be sent up a mountain to breathe, and Brazil's sanatorium era wound down. Campos do Jordão kept the altitude, the cold winters, and the Swiss branding, and turned itself into a winter resort instead. The half-timbered style you see everywhere, especially in the Capivari district, is called enxaimel in Portuguese: exposed wooden beams set horizontally, vertically and diagonally, borrowed from Germany and Switzerland. It is less a heritage than a costume the town chose, and wears very well.

The one thing in the picture that was always there is the tree. The tall, flat-topped, candelabra-shaped conifers on every hillside are araucárias (Araucaria angustifolia), the Paraná pine, native to these highlands between roughly 500 and 1,800 meters. They look like something a dinosaur would lean on, which is fair: their genus goes back to the Triassic. They are also in trouble. The IUCN lists the species as Critically Endangered, after an estimated 97 percent of its original forest was lost over the last century to logging and farmland.

So in a town dressed as Switzerland for Christmas, the most authentic Christmas trees were the ones nobody decorated.

And why the hydrangeas were blue

The walls of hydrangeas along the paths were an almost electric blue. That is soil chemistry, not dye. Hydrangea sepals carry a pigment, delphinidin-3-glucoside, that is pinkish on its own. In acidic soil, aluminum dissolves and the plant pulls it up into the flower, where it locks onto the pigment and turns it blue. In neutral or alkaline soil, the aluminum stays put and the same plant blooms pink. Gardeners call hydrangeas nature's pH meter. In Campos do Jordão, the meter reads very, very acidic.

If you go

  • December is summer, and summer is the rainy season. Daytime highs in the low to mid 20s °C, cool nights, and a lot of afternoon rain, with December, January and February the wettest months. Pack a rain shell and shoes you are happy to get muddy. (Ask me how I know.)
  • Christmas is low season. The crowds come in June and July for the cold. At Christmas the town is decorated and calmer, though weekends and evenings in Capivari still get busy.
  • It is about 170 km from São Paulo, a few hours by car depending on traffic up the serra.
  • Take the train for the ride, not the commute. The 1914 railway from Pindamonhangaba runs tourist services; check the current schedule before you plan around it.
  • Bosque do Silêncio is the easy nature fix. A private park on Avenida Roberto Simonsen, walkable from Vila Capivari, with signposted trails, boardwalks over spring-fed lakes, flowerbeds and paid extras like a treetop course and zipline. Dogs are welcome on a leash. There is an entrance fee; check current prices and hours before you go.
  • Botanique Hotel & Spa is the splurge. Stunning, on a hillside outside town. We booked a spa treatment rather than a stay; check directly with the hotel for what non-guests can book.
  • Bring a dog? We did, and Magnus was welcomed nearly everywhere, including a golf cart. Confirm pet policies with your hotel first.
  • Eat like it's winter anyway. Fondue shops and pancake spots are everywhere. Summer is not a reason to skip the cheese.
  • Look up. The araucárias are protected. Admire them, photograph them, do not take home a souvenir branch.

Muddy and merry

I have spent Christmases in snow and Christmases in heat, and this one was the only one where the town was dressed for one and the weather showed up for the other. It turns out the costume does not matter much. What made it Christmas was pea soup, a fire pit, three muddy beings who love each other, and the people we love on a screen, saying they miss us too.

Miss and love you all.

fieldData.short-version: Campos do Jordão is a mountain town in São Paulo state, about 1,628 m up in the Serra da Mantiqueira, known as the Brazilian Switzerland. It began as a tuberculosis health resort in the late 1800s and became a winter resort after drug treatment ended the sanatorium era. At Christmas it is summer there: mild, green and rainy.
fieldData.quick-answers:
Why is Campos do Jordão called the Brazilian Switzerland?

Its altitude and cold winters drew comparisons to Swiss mountain air when it was a tuberculosis resort, and the town later adopted Alpine-style, half-timbered (enxaimel) architecture as a tourist identity.

What is the weather in Campos do Jordão at Christmas?

December is summer and the rainy season, with mild days in the low to mid 20s °C and cool nights.

Is Campos do Jordão dog friendly?

We traveled with our Samoyed and found it very welcoming; check pet policies with each hotel.

What are the tall umbrella-shaped trees in Campos do Jordão?

Araucárias (Paraná pine), a native, critically endangered conifer.
